title: Pictures of the Trinity
hook: the sun, its light and heat; a lover, a beloved, and love: every picture helps and falls short

segments.voice: Yesterday, all-powerful: almighty, all-knowing, everywhere, and love. Your line was god is love first. Where did you spend a little power on someone else? Day one thousand seventy.

A small green plant, three leaves on one stem. A story people tell says that Saint Patrick, preaching in Ireland, bent down, picked a shamrock, and held it up: three leaves, one plant. Whether it happened, nobody can show. But the story keeps getting told, because it answers a real need. Christians say God is one, and God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and sooner or later somebody asks, how does that work? And somebody reaches for a picture. Today: pictures of the Trinity.

The Trinity is the Christian teaching that there is one God in three persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. The Bible doesn't give a diagram, but it keeps naming the three together. Jesus sends his friends out "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." In the name. One name, three. Paul ends a letter: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all." So teachers reached for pictures. One is the sun: the sun itself, the light that comes from it, and the warmth that reaches your face. One sun, not three, and you never meet the light without the sun. Augustine reached for love. Love needs someone who loves, someone who is loved, and the love between them. Three, and one act of love. And there's Patrick's shamrock. Every one of them helps. And every one falls short. The sun picture can make the Son and the Spirit sound like products of the Father, less than him. The shamrock can make each person sound like a third of God. A popular picture, water as ice, liquid and steam, can make God sound like one person changing costumes, which the creeds reject. The old creed named after Athanasius warns against both mistakes: don't mix up the persons, and don't split the one God into pieces. So teachers keep using pictures, and keep letting them go. It's the same move as the way of not-knowing: a picture opens the door, and then you walk past it.

Here's the practice: draw three circles, overlapping. On paper if you have it, or with a finger on the table, or just in your mind. Three circles, each crossing the other two, with one small shape in the middle where all three meet. Settle, and breathe. Look at the middle. Then look at where the picture breaks: circles have edges, and Christians say God doesn't. Let both be true for a minute. The drawing helps, and it falls short. If you pray, you can pray toward the middle. The bell holds the time.
Pictures of the Trinity. The sun and its light and warmth; a lover, a beloved and love; a shamrock. Each opens a door, and none is the room.
Your line: every picture falls short. Today, when you describe someone you love, notice the moment your words stop fitting them. Day one thousand seventy.

howItsDone: Christians baptize in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and teachers often use pictures like the sun or a shamrock to explain the Trinity, while saying that no picture is the reality.

original.note: Greek: a set of three; the word Greek-speaking Christians used for the Trinity.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Trinity is a riddle with a trick answer.
what it means: one God in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, named together in scripture and pictured many ways.
what a scholar hears: the Athanasian Creed warns against two mistakes, mixing up the persons and dividing the one God. pictures tend to slip into one or the other.

notes: Audit (fresh reviewer): all KJV/BCP quotations checked word for word, attributions and framing checked; no change needed.
Patrick's shamrock is told as 'a story people tell'; it isn't in Patrick's own writings. Confirm the framing.

The sun/light/warmth picture is a common patristic image (e.g. Tertullian, Against Praxeas); not attributed to anyone in the voice. Augustine's lover/beloved/love (On the Trinity VIII.10.14) paraphrased.

Water/ice/steam linked to the error the creeds reject (modalism, not named). Athanasian Creed ('neither confounding the Persons: nor dividing the Substance') paraphrased rather than quoted because of uncertainty over the exact 1662 punctuation. Confirm.
Original: Τριάς (Trias); confirm spelling and accent, and the pronunciation.
